[](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/139498135/647550183/1231236074?refcode=RS_EM_FR_2026.09.18_Olivia&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMDIvMS82NzI5OCIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICJjYjMzNzdjOS1hZmIzLWYxMTEtYTZhNy0wMDIyNDgyYTlhOGQiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=mVwu1iuwquFYnN4bBRGqSYRN2Lfl5gAwEidndL4zlko=&emci=c9700230-a5b3-f111-a6a7-0022482a9a8d&emdi=cb3377c9-afb3-f111-a6a7-0022482a9a8d&ceid=23483442) | Hey, Peter, I want to get a little personal. I’m going to talk to you about my sister Olivia, because Olivia’s story is such an important part of the work I do. [](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/139498136/647550184/1133857793?refcode=RS_EM_FR_2026.09.18_Olivia&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMDIvMS82NzI5OCIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICJjYjMzNzdjOS1hZmIzLWYxMTEtYTZhNy0wMDIyNDgyYTlhOGQiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=mVwu1iuwquFYnN4bBRGqSYRN2Lfl5gAwEidndL4zlko=) Olivia was born with microcephaly, which meant her head and brain were smaller than expected. From the very beginning, she needed complex medical care, surgeries, and equipment — a wheelchair, feeding pumps, a nebulizer, and more. While my dad’s Union job provided health insurance — it didn’t cover everything Olivia needed. **Medicaid helped fill that gap and made it possible for our family to give Olivia the care she deserved** — from medical equipment and appointments at Mary Bridge and Tacoma General to home visits from early intervention specialists, nurses, and therapists. _I learned at a young age that the decisions lawmakers make can have a profound impact on whether families like mine can get the care they need._ Today, I fight to protect Medicaid because I know firsthand what it can mean for a family. The Republican controlled Congress is putting that care at risk, and we have to make sure families don’t lose access to the programs they rely on. But we can’t reverse that damage if we don’t flip the House in November — that’s why I’m writing to you. I need your help. [**What you donate here, I’m sending to campaigns in tough to win districts across the country. Can you pitch in?**](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/139498137/647550185/1133857793?refcode=RS_EM_FR_2026.09.18_Olivia&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMDIvMS82NzI5OCIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICJjYjMzNzdjOS1hZmIzLWYxMTEtYTZhNy0wMDIyNDgyYTlhOGQiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=mVwu1iuwquFYnN4bBRGqSYRN2Lfl5gAwEidndL4zlko=) If you've saved payment information with ActBlue Express, your donation will go through immediately: [EXPRESS DONATE: $10](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/139498138/647550186/-1265565946?amount=10&refcode=RS_EM_FR_2026.09.18_Olivia&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMDIvMS82NzI5OCIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICJjYjMzNzdjOS1hZmIzLWYxMTEtYTZhNy0wMDIyNDgyYTlhOGQiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=mVwu1iuwquFYnN4bBRGqSYRN2Lfl5gAwEidndL4zlko=) [EXPRESS DONATE: $25](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/139498139/647550187/-1265565946?amount=25&express_lane=true&refcode=RS_EM_FR_2026.09.18_Olivia&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMDIvMS82NzI5OCIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICJjYjMzNzdjOS1hZmIzLWYxMTEtYTZhNy0wMDIyNDgyYTlhOGQiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=mVwu1iuwquFYnN4bBRGqSYRN2Lfl5gAwEidndL4zlko=) [EXPRESS DONATE: $50](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/139498140/647550188/-1265565946?amount=50&express_lane=true&refcode=RS_EM_FR_2026.09.18_Olivia&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMDIvMS82NzI5OCIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICJjYjMzNzdjOS1hZmIzLWYxMTEtYTZhNy0wMDIyNDgyYTlhOGQiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=mVwu1iuwquFYnN4bBRGqSYRN2Lfl5gAwEidndL4zlko=) Being Olivia’s big sister also meant becoming a caregiver. I helped change her diapers. I hooked up her feeding tube. I made sure she got her medication. And I would hold her hand when she had seizures. While my dad’s Union job provided health insurance — it didn’t cover everything Olivia needed. Medicaid helped fill that gap and made it possible for our family to give Olivia the care she deserved — from medical equipment and appointments at Mary Bridge and Tacoma General to home visits from early intervention specialists, nurses, and therapists. U.S. Senator Katie Britt addressed a standing-room-only crowd of Alabama business leaders Wednesday at the Alabama Business Coalition’s September member meeting in Washington, D.C., where she outlined the outlook for defense appropriations, artificial intelligence legislation, and children’s online safety in the final weeks before the end of the fiscal year. The meeting, sponsored by The University of Alabama System, also featured Dr. Peter Mohler, President of The University of Alabama, who discussed the role of higher education in Alabama’s workforce development and economic growth.

The U.S. House of Representatives passed legislation Wednesday to impose new sanctions against Russia and extend current sanctions against Iran. The bill, which late U.S. Senator Lindsey Graham advocated for and now bears his name, passed 262-159 and will go to President Trump’s desk, where he is expected to sign it into law. After the bill’s passage, a bipartisan, bicameral group of lawmakers held a press conference to celebrate the sanctions. U.S. Senator Katie Britt, R-Alabama, attended.

U.S. Sen. Katie Britt (R-Montgomery) lauded the recent efforts of the Trump administration for helping fight against crime in the Yellowhammer State. FBI Director Kash Patel testified in front of the Senate Tuesday, and discussed Operation Southern Star, which targeted violent crime in the Montgomery area. “The operation Southern Star was so successful. I think within two weeks, you made 63 arrests, 52 guns, 40 drug seizures. There was real accountability,” Britt said to Patel during the hearing. “Since then, I’ve continued to be impressed.”

clean_body: | | | | | | | U.S. Senator Katie Britt addressed a standing-room-only crowd of Alabama business leaders Wednesday at the Alabama Business Coalition’s September member meeting in Washington, D.C., where she outlined the outlook for defense appropriations, artificial intelligence legislation, and children’s online safety in the final weeks before the end of the fiscal year. The meeting, sponsored by The University of Alabama System, also featured Dr. Peter Mohler, President of The University of Alabama, who discussed the role of higher education in Alabama’s workforce development and economic growth. | | The U.S. House of Representatives passed legislation Wednesday to impose new sanctions against Russia and extend current sanctions against Iran. The bill, which late U.S. Senator Lindsey Graham advocated for and now bears his name, passed 262-159 and will go to President Trump’s desk, where he is expected to sign it into law. After the bill’s passage, a bipartisan, bicameral group of lawmakers held a press conference to celebrate the sanctions. U.S. Senator Katie Britt, R-Alabama, attended. | | U.S. Sen. Katie Britt (R-Montgomery) lauded the recent efforts of the Trump administration for helping fight against crime in the Yellowhammer State. FBI Director Kash Patel testified in front of the Senate Tuesday, and discussed Operation Southern Star, which targeted violent crime in the Montgomery area. “The operation Southern Star was so successful. | | **Election Highlights**
---
| **Delaware**
* [Chris Coons](https://us.list-manage.com/bte1iRmTU5S?e=d6c5c7d7ec&c2id=d01ae369e8fbc8d507a43d27c2d1769e) clinched the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate in Delaware.

**Massachusetts**
* [Ed Markey](https://us.list-manage.com/CxEBZv0zoNN?e=d6c5c7d7ec&c2id=d01ae369e8fbc8d507a43d27c2d1769e) won the Democratic primary for U.S. Senate in Massachusetts.
* [Maura Healey](https://us.list-manage.com/tJvfSbQlKky?e=d6c5c7d7ec&c2id=d01ae369e8fbc8d507a43d27c2d1769e) clinched the Democratic nomination to serve a second term as governor of Massachusetts.

**New Hampshire**
* [Chris Pappas](https://us.list-manage.com/xcqBVgmTnZe?e=d6c5c7d7ec&c2id=d01ae369e8fbc8d507a43d27c2d1769e) won the Democratic primary for U.S. Senate in New Hampshire.
* [Cinde Warmington ](https://us.list-manage.com/hgRhlJOlmWu?e=d6c5c7d7ec&c2id=d01ae369e8fbc8d507a43d27c2d1769e)clinched the Democratic nomination for governor of New Hampshire.

**Oklahoma**
* [N’kiyla Jasmine Thomas](https://us.list-manage.com/141kal0x7tr?e=d6c5c7d7ec&c2id=d01ae369e8fbc8d507a43d27c2d1769e) won the Democratic primary runoff for U.S. Senate in Oklahoma.

**Rhode Island**
* [Jack Reed ](https://us.list-manage.com/UBDoujHyuYA?e=d6c5c7d7ec&c2id=d01ae369e8fbc8d507a43d27c2d1769e)clinched the Democratic nomination to serve another term as U.S. Senator from Rhode Island.
* [Helena Foulkes](https://us.list-manage.com/11jjFKEsmJ_?e=d6c5c7d7ec&c2id=d01ae369e8fbc8d507a43d27c2d1769e) won the Democratic primary for governor of Rhode Island.

# **Get Out the Vote!**
The DNC is seeking experienced former campaigners to fill key Late Help roles in key battleground states for the 2026 elections to regain control of the U.S. House and Senate. Your experience matters greatly!

**KEY DETAILS**
* **Role Format:** Primarily in-person on the ground, with limited remote opportunities.
* **Experience:** Organizing, GOTV, Operations, Data, Voter Protection, IT, Comms.
* **Locations:** AZ, GA, MI, NC, NV, PA, WI, etc., with flexible options.

| In August, the [DNC launched an unprecedented voter registration program in Nevada](https://us.list-manage.com/hPx5IvTAT1L?e=d6c5c7d7ec&c2id=d01ae369e8fbc8d507a43d27c2d1769e) as it invests in reaching, mobilizing, and turning out young Democrats across the Silver State ahead of the critical midterm elections.

As part of the DNC’s historic partisan voter registration effort, dozens of When We Count fellows will conduct on-the-ground voter registration drives at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas — one of the most diverse colleges in the country — in addition to registering voters at community meetings and outside of sporting events, concerts, stores, and festivals.
---
|
---
| **Organizing Everywhere: Local Listeners Recap**
---
| [ ](https://us.list-manage.com/jH06pSzINV0?e=d6c5c7d7ec&c2id=d01ae369e8fbc8d507a43d27c2d1769e)
---
| This year, more than 400 volunteers joined us to make 448,295 calls to voters who voted in 2020, but not 2024.
* We had nearly 10,000 conversations with voters from 61 battleground districts across the country, and what we found could change the game for the midterms.
* 78% of voters said the country is headed in the wrong direction under Trump, with the rising cost of living being their top priority issue.
* Voters want leaders who fight for them, their families, and their communities.
* 86% of these voters explicitly stated that they plan to vote in the upcoming midterm elections this November.

These conversations don't just allow us to sway people in key districts — they help us build back vital trust that Democrats may have lost in recent years.
---
| [Learn More About Our Findings](https://us.list-manage.com/C9erTwZM3Rt?e=d6c5c7d7ec&c2id=d01ae369e8fbc8d507a43d27c2d1769e "Learn More About Our Findings")

|
---
**Meet Wendy Celaya**

Wendy Celaya, a Los Angeles native and community advocate, serves on various city boards and initiatives. She volunteers with the California Democratic Party and Los Angeles County Democratic Party, promoting voter engagement and civic participation. Wendy leads voter-protection training and develops community canvassing programs connecting residents to civic resources. In 2016, she worked with the Hillary Victory Fund, gaining experience in civic engagement. For a decade, she has volunteered with the Los Angeles Mission and Anne Douglas Center, leading a pro bono legal clinic to help individuals overcome legal barriers to employment and housing. She currently serves as a commissioner on the Los Angeles County Local Agency Formation Commission, supporting regional governance.

name: Rep Mark Takano and OnePA
subject: It’s time for a 4 day work week
body:
It’s time to redefine full-time work | |
---
Peter, **** For over 80 years, America's standard work week has been stuck at 40 hours, even though **workers are 400% more productive today than in the 1940s.** While technology, automation, and innovation have transformed our economy, working people have been left behind. _Instead, we're working longer hours for lower wages, sacrificing time with our families, and burning out at unprecedented rates._ That's why I'm proud to introduce the **_Thirty-Two Hour Workweek Act_** , transformative legislation that will finally bring our work standards into the 21st century. [**If you think it’s time that our labor laws reflect the moment, then add your name as a supporter of the bill for a 32-hr work week!**](https://click.actionnetwork.org/ss/c/u001.qUXRBnqZ7T8nxbpAcIVwoUsWLkUMWlo_0JmZttSlm38TprM8-zgydfLp8z7CCTwPWLYbTULTNgZ48k_EeMXI8Yw5LuCEKzFEO4xiORf1iroK9jFSWtvkQIgHCRXtG84rajWNpGE_uCbBo4GXMDUVVMOT0ohH702mk-HcxsC3DDiVrUp4tfXsjTTYRUv6LZAbE8eqbvP8Weu14w_cKB2kIrIht5pRcAHFJVACdRbmcaW4-8PUf5Ky06FOmhCSiTQzxmdfD-P-NYG_8Vcf4XjtNnctQdwabbycb8zZu-P6sWrz24wP0c9vl0ABaBiQHZ2O2PB0JEN8v862XPyf0K_UR55X_--wNlNy-PvfjrUHlRdF13r7uWjs2t9O3HW7pemGSyc3eDyMeslqybE-dUy7amzrqGgWlwnFV8FIga5xH7Obl8XFR7yWmFTUizzHZjV_VhD6rhiUO9w9UQ5THDABGA/4u5/2WdP3nzdQwOr9DzJbfDbzQ/h0/h001.sylCIoJP-_xNBllM1aOn1ViEuLBDJ90NeKd7zk1NE98) | | [ACT NOW](https://click.actionnetwork.org/ss/c/u001.qUXRBnqZ7T8nxbpAcIVwoUsWLkUMWlo_0JmZttSlm38TprM8-zgydfLp8z7CCTwPWLYbTULTNgZ48k_EeMXI8Yw5LuCEKzFEO4xiORf1iroK9jFSWtvkQIgHCRXtG84rajWNpGE_uCbBo4GXMDUVVMOT0ohH702mk-HcxsC3DDiVrUp4tfXsjTTYRUv6LZAbE8eqbvP8Weu14w_cKB2kIrIht5pRcAHFJVACdRbmcaU4jvIdgx2Vi1NVz5B0CN-2CSqRp-ve59vGreJm0Nymf8QMAIh88mxkprAeI2_bbunydY-aPHTTrFyiEOElMslnFaZt_FOGZELVegB5w1Kb_qigNXJ4rV_aflLmWeiTZkD5CH_Vp1zXBsh6QnD9B8c9kzhLSj7aGkisVlN3D1ZGxMFyJ7O6rPH4gFnY0CamXFApFfiazAWMki-NOTEPTjltEmDJjkrb2SMSTV_-YZU5mg/4u5/2WdP3nzdQwOr9DzJbfDbzQ/h1/h001.zhDrccpLq4mq16awwEse2ErXIz_vzt1nkzs37_V9IY4)
---
****
The Thirty-Two Hour Workweek Act will:

* **Reduce the standard workweek from 40 hours to 32 hours** over a three-year phase-in period
* **Require overtime pay after 32 hours** for non-exempt employees
* **Guarantee no loss of pay for workers** transitioning to a shorter week
* **Encourage employers to either shorten workweeks or pay overtime** , putting power back in workers' hands

The evidence is clear:**shorter workweeks improve health, boost productivity, and strengthen families.** Pilot programs around the world show that when workers have more time to rest, recharge, and spend with loved ones, everyone wins – including businesses.

Welcome to Adam Hamilton for Kansas
Don't recognize this sender? [Unsubscribe with one click](https://substack..OEcldb2rUhzY_VrdZ_ScBu8f6cFwdkANQltlfFC1XLs?)
Adam Hamilton for Kansas recently imported your email address from another platform to Substack. You'll now receive their posts via email or the [Substack app](https://link.sbstck.com/redirect/ec04c56d-6c96-4807-b27c-74d6eaa7e710?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). To set up your profile and discover more on Substack, [click here](https://link.sbstck.com/redirect/212d30b8-f360-4e31-84c7-340f59a6db73?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
Not too long ago, I went to Liberal, Kansas. I asked some people what the best sights were to see while I was in town. All of them pointed me to Dorothy's House and the Land of Oz Museum. They were right: It was a blast.
It's probably been 20 years since I've seen the movie, but it all came flooding back when I watched a clip they were playing.
In the scene, Dorothy and Toto were on their way to find the Wizard. Heading down the Yellow Brick Road with them were her three trusty sidekicks: the Scarecrow, the Tin Man and the Cowardly Lion.
Each of them, as you probably remember, were seeking something different from the Wizard:
The Scarecrow needed a brain.
The Tin Man needed a heart.
And the Cowardly Lion? He needed courage.
I couldn't help it -- I had to laugh. It's the _perfect_ metaphor for what's wrong in Washington today!
Folks, we've got a lot of politicians in D.C. right now who have _lost their minds._ They've stopped using their brains to solve problems. Instead, they're doing whatever the president or their party tells them to do.
**That 's not good for Kansas or the country.**
We've got a lot of leaders who have lost their hearts too. If you live like Roger Marshall, I guess you can see how it would be easy to do: Go to Washington. Live there for 185 days. Go to Florida for a while. Then, come back to Kansas to get some photo ops in front of Cabela's or wherever, but don't actually spend more than five minutes with the people there. Don't _listen_. Get your picture taken and move on.
That's what my opponent does. The last time he held a listening session -- over 560 days ago, I might add -- he got upset at what people were saying and walked out. Then, he said he wasn't going to have listening sessions anymore, because people are too "dangerous" and listening sessions are "non-productive."
**I 've talked to a lot of Kansans. We aren't dangerous, even when we disagree. But we do have some very real challenges that need to be addressed. That's what my opponent fails to understand: Listening to people is the only way to represent them.**
When you listen to people, you feel their pain. You hear their suffering. And you say, "I have to do something about this. I can't vote for things that take health insurance away from 51,000 Kansans. I can't support a policy that leaves 18,000 children without food assistance." Your heart won't let you.
To make things even worse, far too many people in Washington have lost their courage right along with their brains and their hearts. They won't stand up to the president or their party and say, "This is hurting people back home." Kansas -- and the country -- needs leaders who are courageous enough to fight, even if the president bullies them, calls them names or picks on them. A leader's duty is to their people. Backing down in the face of scare tactics is not OK.
**Kansans need a leader who will use their brain to make good decisions. Who will open their heart to their pain. Who will have the courage to help them, even when it goes against what the administration and corporate lobbyists want.**
**If I 'm elected, that's exactly what I'll do. But I need your help to stay in the fight. [Please, will you rush your gift today to help me beat Roger Marshall in November and start standing up for Kansans?](https://link.sbstck.com/redirect/9d794d44-e118-49cd-ac2e-6439ab0d5a57?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**

Thanks for standing with me,
Adam

Adam Hamilton for Kansas recently imported your email address from another platform to Substack. You'll now receive their posts via email or the . To set up your profile and discover more on Substack, . Not too long ago, I went to Liberal, Kansas. I asked some people what the best sights were to see while I was in town. All of them pointed me to Dorothy's House and the Land of Oz Museum. They were right: It was a blast. It's probably been 20 years since I've seen the movie, but it all came flooding back when I watched a clip they were playing. In the scene, Dorothy and Toto were on their way to find the Wizard. Heading down the Yellow Brick Road with them were her three trusty sidekicks: the Scarecrow, the Tin Man and the Cowardly Lion. Each of them, as you probably remember, were seeking something different from the Wizard: The Scarecrow needed a brain. The Tin Man needed a heart. And the Cowardly Lion? He needed courage. I couldn't help it -- I had to laugh. It's the perfect metaphor for what's wrong in Washington today! Folks, we've got a lot of politicians in D.C. right now who have lost their minds. They've stopped using their brains to solve problems. Instead, they're doing whatever the president or their party tells them to do. That 's not good for Kansas or the country. We've got a lot of leaders who have lost their hearts too. If you live like Roger Marshall, I guess you can see how it would be easy to do: Go to Washington. Live there for 185 days. Go to Florida for a while. Then, come back to Kansas to get some photo ops in front of Cabela's or wherever, but don't actually spend more than five minutes with the people there. Don't listen. Get your picture taken and move on. That's what my opponent does. The last time he held a listening session -- over 560 days ago, I might add -- he got upset at what people were saying and walked out. Then, he said he wasn't going to have listening sessions anymore, because people are too "dangerous" and listening sessions are "non-productive." I 've talked to a lot of Kansans. We aren't dangerous, even when we disagree. But we do have some very real challenges that need to be addressed. That's what my opponent fails to understand: Listening to people is the only way to represent them. When you listen to people, you feel their pain. You hear their suffering. And you say, "I have to do something about this. I can't vote for things that take health insurance away from 51,000 Kansans. I can't support a policy that leaves 18,000 children without food assistance." Your heart won't let you. To make things even worse, far too many people in Washington have lost their courage right along with their brains and their hearts. They won't stand up to the president or their party and say, "This is hurting people back home." Kansas -- and the country -- needs leaders who are courageous enough to fight, even if the president bullies them, calls them names or picks on them. A leader's duty is to their people. Backing down in the face of scare tactics is not OK. Kansans need a leader who will use their brain to make good decisions. Who will open their heart to their pain. Who will have the courage to help them, even when it goes against what the administration and corporate lobbyists want. If I 'm elected, that's exactly what I'll do. But I need your help to stay in the fight. Thanks for standing with me, Adam | | | | | | | (C) 2026 Adam Hamilton for Kansas 548 Market Street PMB 72296, San Francisco, CA 94104 ? ?

Washington has a vocabulary problem. Let's start there.
Every few years, a new administration announces another "economic onslaught." Another "financial stranglehold." Another "maximum pressure campaign."
This time it is Iran, and the language coming out of Treasury recently has been almost cinematic: an "economic D-Day," a promise to sever "every economic lifeline" sustaining the regime.
It is the same tone Mike Pompeo used in 2018, promising Iran "the strongest sanctions in history." It is the same register Barack Obama used in 2012, promising "even more crippling sanctions." Different administrations, different parties, the same metaphor: **suffocation**.
But suffocation is a _method_. It is **not an objective**. And a superpower that stops asking the difference is not being tough; **it is being lazy.**
* * *
Economic sanctions can do several different jobs. They can constrain access to weapons, technology, capital, or strategic inputs. They can deter third parties from assisting prohibited activity. They can freeze assets, disrupt patronage networks, signal international condemnation, or raise the cost of aggression. Sometimes those measures work even when the target government never changes its mind.
But maximum-pressure campaigns make a larger claim. Their theory is not merely that economic restrictions will deny a particular component or interrupt a particular transaction. Their theory is that **sufficiently severe economic pressure will change the political decisions of the targeted state.**
That is the claim we should evaluate on its merits.
The question was never _can America hurt Iran 's economy?_ Obviously yes. Iran's GDP is projected to contract by more than five percent this year. Inflation climbed from the low 50s to nearly 90% in a matter of months. The rial has collapsed in exchange rate value below **two million** to the dollar. That is real economic pain, and it is landing as serious poverty on millions of real families.
The question that we're looking at today, is different, and it's the one the planners in in DC should have been evaluating this whole time: _**what political outcome do we intend for that suffering to produce, and why do we believe hurting these particular people will produce it?**_
Increasingly, the answer appears to be that the transmission mechanism DC has been counting on **is badly broken.** Meaning, the US is inflicting mass suffering, on purpose, with no discernible strategic value, and no anticipated endpoint, at immense cost both to the Iranian people and to our moral and strategic position in the world.
**And we should know better.** We've run versions of this experiment before, at enormous cost, without absorbing what they should have taught us.
Let's get into it.

## Morality and strategy belong in the same room
There is a habit in American foreign policy of treating the humanitarian objection as the "soft" one, the thing people raise when they have not quite grasped how power works. I want to reject that framing directly, because it gets the relationship between morality and strategy almost exactly backwards.
Morality without strategy is useless sentiment. It can feel righteous and change nothing. Strategy without morality curdles into something worse than useless: **callous cruelty wearing the costume of realism.** Good statecraft requires both halves -- a legitimate objective and a method capable of reaching it at a cost proportionate to what can actually be gained.
Ask a strategist what they need to know before backing a coercive policy, and the list should sound reasonably familiar. _What is the objective? What mechanism connects this action to that objective? Who actually absorbs the cost? How will the adversary adapt? What happens to our alliances, credibility, and freedom of action along the way? At what point does the human toll exceed any plausible strategic return?_
Now ask the moral questions. _Is the harm necessary? Is it falling primarily on people responsible for the conduct we are trying to change? Is the cost proportionate to the objective? Is there a less destructive means available? Is there a reasonable prospect of success?_
Those are not competing frameworks. Necessity, discrimination, proportionality, and a reasonable prospect of success sound like moral criteria because they are. They also sound remarkably like **competent planning.**
Moral discipline is, among other things, a technology for preventing strategic stupidity.
If your plan requires millions of civilians to suffer in the hope that their suffering will eventually change someone else's decision, asking whether that mechanism actually _**works**_ is not sentimentality. It is the first question any serious strategist should ask.

## Iran: a state that learned to survive the blow
Here is what the data on Iran's economy shows once you look past the headline numbers.
**Iran has spent more than a decade adapting to severe economic pressure.** Before the current war, it kept oil flowing to China through sanctions-evasion networks. Currency depreciation made Iranian goods cheaper across the region, turning one economic weakness into an export advantage. Iranian firms, especially in sensitive industries such as electrical machinery, built inventories that can run close to 200 days deep. A blockade therefore does not necessarily stop production immediately; it begins by drawing down reserves accumulated for exactly this kind of disruption.
Iranian policymakers also followed a very different path from Moscow. When Russia was hit with major sanctions after invading Ukraine, it responded with fiscal stimulus, industrial expansion, tighter labor markets, and rising wages -- something approaching a wartime mobilization of the domestic economy. Iran, on the other hand,
tolerated inflation, ran austerity budgets, allowed weak labor conditions to suppress wages, and did relatively little to protect household purchasing power. It also declined to impose the kind of price controls that had helped shield civilians during the Iran-Iraq War.
Whether every part of this outcome was deliberately engineered matters less than the fact that Iranian leaders have repeatedly demonstrated their willingness to tolerate it.
The economic burden that DC is intending to impose on the capacity of decisionmakers in Tehran to maintain Iran's sovereignty, has instead migrated downward onto ordinary people.
Households buy less. Firms pass costs onto consumers. People rely increasingly on credit and informal loans. Even food retailers report falling sales volume -- never a good sign. Meanwhile, the state has preserved greater access to the resources it considers essential.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/4a826352-a030-4d10-aa30-288b2e433263?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
The result is a genuinely ugly, but resilient, equilibrium. As households consume less, Iran needs fewer imports. As import demand falls, the state needs less foreign currency to keep the remaining economy functioning. Imports are on pace to fall from roughly $72 billion two years ago to around $40 billion this year.
That is evidence of impoverishment. It is also, mechanically, one of the things allowing the system to remain functional while its people absorb the loss.
None of that means sanctions have no effect. They damage growth, industrial development, household welfare, and Iran's long-term economic capacity. They can constrain access to particular goods and technologies. **But none of those effects establishes that broad economic suffering will compel Tehran to make the political concessions Washington seeks.**
A country can become much poorer without becoming much more compliant.

## Pain is not leverage unless someone can transmit it
This is the causal mechanism that too often disappears inside the phrase "economic pressure."
Sanctions do not coerce governments by magic. Pressure has to travel through a political system. The implicit chain looks something like this: economic restrictions create losses; those losses fall on politically relevant actors; those actors pressure the leadership; the leadership concludes that continuing the challenged policy costs more than changing it; behavior changes.
**Break any link in that chain, and more pain does not necessarily produce more leverage.**
Authoritarian systems are unusually capable of breaking those links. They can shift scarcity toward households, protect favored constituencies, ration access to hard currency, suppress protest, censor information, scapegoat outsiders, and use coercive institutions to prevent public discontent from becoming elite constraint. **They may be economically damaged while remaining politically insulated.**
That produces a fundamental problem for coercive strategy. The governments most willing to let their own citizens suffer are often the governments least susceptible to a strategy that depends on civilian suffering becoming politically intolerable.
Sanctions generate pressure. **Political transmission converts pressure into leverage.** If the political system can prevent that pressure from reaching the people who make the decisions, increasing the pressure may increase suffering without increasing leverage.
Iran is not the first place the US should have learned this.

## Iraq: the warning was more complicated -- and worse
Iraq is not a simple story in which sanctions accomplished nothing. Saying so would make the argument easier to write and easier to knock down.
After Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait in 1990, the UN Security Council imposed one of the most comprehensive sanctions regimes of the modern era. Following the Gulf War, sanctions became tied to Iraqi compliance with disarmament obligations and an intrusive international inspection regime.
Those measures did constrain Saddam Hussein's capabilities. Combined with inspections, international monitoring, and the threat of military force, they contributed to the dismantlement and degradation of weapons programs that Washington would later badly misunderstand.
From a cold strategic perspective, the sanctions were partially effective.
But look at the cost.
Sanctions on Iraq remained in place, in varying forms, for **thirteen years**. Iraqi economic and civic life deteriorated so severely that the international community created the Oil-for-Food program to mitigate the humanitarian consequences while attempting to preserve strategic pressure. Saddam's government contributed substantially to the catastrophe through repression, corruption, misallocation, and its manipulation of relief. The destruction of the Gulf War and Iraq's degraded infrastructure compounded the damage.
**But the central political fact remained: Saddam Hussein stayed in power.**
That should have forced a harder conversation about what exactly the sanctions regime was accomplishing and at what price. It constrained Iraqi state capacity, but it did not reliably convert civilian deprivation into political moderation. It helped contain weapons programs, yet by 2003 the United States still invaded Iraq professing a belief that Saddam possessed prohibited stockpiles -- that in fact, were not there.
A coercive system partly designed to produce disarmament helped produce substantial disarmament. **Yet --** the target state remained authoritarian, the population endured extraordinary hardship, international confidence in the regime frayed, and the system ultimately failed to generate enough trusted information or political resolution to prevent a disastrous war premised on a false assessment of the very threat the policy had helped constrain.
The lesson is not simply that sanctions are hard on civilians. It is that strategic success cannot be measured by economic damage alone, and that even genuine success along one dimension does not erase catastrophic failure along others.
The larger structural problem remains. Comprehensive economic coercion often assumes that a government will change course when the suffering of its population becomes sufficiently severe. **The more ruthless and insulated the government, the weaker that assumption becomes.**
We therefore have a recurring habit of choosing one of our harshest tools against exactly the governments _**least**_ constrained by moral duty to their people.

## Cuba: sixty years is no longer an experiment
If Iraq shows how coercion can generate a mixture of real constraint and enormous failure within a single brutal decade, Cuba shows what policy inertia looks like once it has had more than sixty years to harden.
The United States imposed the core of its embargo on Cuba **in the early 1960s.** American objectives have shifted over the decades: removing or isolating Castro's government, limiting Soviet influence, promoting democratization, pressing for human rights, securing political reform, and conditioning normalization on changes inside Cuba.
The goalposts have been moved repeatedly. Yet the instrument has stayed remarkably consistent. **Why?**
At some point, a policy that has failed to produce its central political ambitions for longer than most Americans have been alive stops being an experiment and starts becoming an identity.
The legitimacy cost has compounded alongside it. In October 2025, the UN General Assembly voted for the thirty-third consecutive year to call for the embargo's end: 165 countries in favor, 7 against, and 12 abstaining. That is not a hippie protest. **It is most of the world, year after year, telling DC that it regards the policy as cruel, harmful, illegitimate, counterproductive, or all of the above.**
None of this requires absolving Havana. Cuba's government has made catastrophic economic decisions of its own and has a long record of repressing its citizens. Both things can be true simultaneously. The relevant question for American policymakers was never whether the Cuban government deserved criticism. It was **whether decades of American economic punishment would achieve the political transformations used to justify it.**
They have not.
And in the meantime, the embargo handed Havana something politically useful: **a real, provable, external antagonist**. Every domestic failure can be attributed to DC in public messaging -- often accurately, sometimes deliberately inaccurately as a smokescreen for domestic policy failures -- usually in proportions the average citizen has little ability to disentangle.
That is a strategic gift to an authoritarian government.

## When the three failures become one
Put Iran, Iraq, and Cuba beside one another and a larger pattern emerges.
The first failure is **humanitarian**. People who neither made nor control the policies being punished lose purchasing power, food security, medicine, jobs, savings, economic mobility, and the ordinary predictability on which family life depends. If that's not collective punishment, what is?
The second is **strategic failure**. The targeted state adapts. It protects favored resources, reroutes trade, represses dissent, finds alternative partners, absorbs the losses it can absorb, and pushes the remainder outward and downward. Sometimes it survives for decades.
The third is a **failure of legitimacy.** Everyone else is watching, and they draw conclusions about how the United States uses power, whether DC can be trusted, and whether they might be next.
**That third failure feeds the second**. America's ability to organize coalitions depends largely on other governments believing that we exercise power with restraint, that our stated rules are more than convenient rhetoric, that civilian welfare actually enters into our decisions, and that cooperation with us does not mean surrendering indefinitely to whatever policy Washington may choose next.
**Moral credibility is not decorative trim on American power. It is a core, structural part of American power.**
Countries cooperate with us not only because we are strong, but because alliances, institutions, law, reputation, trust, and perceived legitimacy reduce the cost of getting other actors to move with us.
**Legitimacy is force multiplication. Hypocrisy creates strategic friction.**
If the visible result of American policy is that ordinary people become markedly poorer while the target government retains enough power to continue the conduct we intended to stop, other countries do not need to adopt Tehran's worldview to question Washington's judgment.

## The bill comes due somewhere else
The same problem reaches beyond the targeted country.
When Washington leans heavily on dollar dominance, correspondent banking, market access, and secondary sanctions as instruments of coercion, other governments are not only asking whether Iran deserves the pressure. They are also asking what their own dependence on American-controlled financial infrastructure could mean under a future disagreement.
That anxiety now appears regularly in BRICS diplomacy and throughout parts of the Global South. At the most recent summit, BRICS leaders again condemned unilateral sanctions imposed outside the framework of the UN Security Council. The declaration did not name Washington, but American and Western sanctions architecture has long been one of the grievances animating that conversation.
BRICS countries are not a unified anti-American bloc. India, Brazil, South Africa, China, Russia, and the bloc's newer members have different interests and often different views of the international order. Nor is the dollar about to vanish, although several meaningful global trade structures are being built to reduce global dependency on financial infrastructure DC controls.
Bottom line: **every American use of financial dominance as a weapon teaches other governments something about the risk of depending on the system through which that weapon operates.**
The rational response is diversification: more local-currency settlement, more alternative payment infrastructure, more trading relationships insulated from Western jurisdiction, more reserve diversification, and more political interest in institutions Washington cannot easily control.
Whether or not this leads to a sudden collapse of dollar dominance, it is clearly a long-term strategic cost. We are spending down our strongest global form of enduring power carelessly, even recklessly, and assuming we can go on doing so forever.
That's foolish. America is spending financial leverage faster than we are rebuilding the legitimacy that helps sustain it.

## The dictator's bargain
Across Iraq, Cuba, and now Iran, the same political mechanism keeps appearing.
Washington tells the population: **your suffering is your government 's fault.** The government tells its population: **your suffering is Washington 's fault.** Frustratingly, both sides can often produce evidence.
The authoritarian government made bad choices, repressed its population, distorted its economy, or pursued policies that invited external pressure. The outside power then imposed policies that made ordinary life materially worse. One source of suffering does not erase the other.
**That ambiguity is a gift to authoritarian rulers.** It gives them an external villain who is at least partly real.
It also exposes a contradiction in the coercive theory. _We tell an oppressed population that its government does not care whether it suffers, and then make civilian economic suffering a central mechanism by which we expect that government to change its behavior._
The less accountable the government is to its population, the weaker that transmission mechanism becomes.
This does not mean authoritarian leaders are immune to economic pressure. They care about elite cohesion, patronage networks, military capability, state revenue, access to strategic technology, and their own survival. Those are real pressure points.
But that is exactly why serious strategy should identify and attack the relevant pressure point specifically, rather than treating generalized national misery as a proxy for leverage.

## What better strategy actually looks like
None of this is an argument for unilateral disarmament, and it should not be mistaken for one. States sometimes need coercive tools. Sanctions can constrain dangerous capabilities, freeze assets, raise costs, disrupt procurement, punish specific actors, and support broader diplomatic or security objectives.
The requirement is more demanding than "targeted sanctions good, broad sanctions bad." Targeted measures are often more defensible because they discriminate better between decision-makers and civilians, but they are not automatically effective at compelling political change.
The real principle is simpler: **match the instrument to the mechanism.**
If the objective is to prevent acquisition of a weapons component, target the component, supplier, financing channel, and logistics network. If the objective is to disrupt elite patronage, target the assets and institutions on which that patronage depends. If the objective is to change behavior, identify the person or coalition capable of changing it and build pressure around what that actor values.
**Then build an off-ramp.**
A coercive policy without a credible path to relief easily becomes punishment without strategy. The target must know what behavior is being demanded, what compliance would look like, what partial compliance earns, and what actions actually cause sanctions to end.
Otherwise the pressure tends to become permanent -- because permanence is bureaucratically easier than declaring success, admitting failure, or renegotiating the objective.
**Humanitarian protections also have to work outside the text of a Treasury regulation.** Formal exemptions for food and medicine are not enough if banks, insurers, freight companies, pharmaceutical suppliers, and intermediaries conclude that touching the sanctioned economy creates unacceptable compliance risk. A humanitarian exemption that no functioning financial institution is willing to process is an exemption on paper, not a real humanitarian channel that helps people.
Protected payment mechanisms, credible safe harbors, clear licensing, and active monitoring of real-world access have to be part of the design.
And every major sanctions regime should face periodic review -- scheduled, not optional -- built around questions so obvious that it is remarkable how rarely they organize the public debate: _Who exactly must change what behavior? Why should this specific pressure make that actor change it? Who is actually absorbing the cost? What capabilities are being constrained? What evidence would show that the policy is succeeding? What evidence would show that it is failing? What is the humanitarian ceiling? What is the exit condition?_
If the architects cannot answer those questions, that is an answer.

## A superpower capable of restraint
A superpower does not prove its strength by demonstrating that it can impoverish people who cannot meaningfully fight back. We already know we can do that. Everyone knows we can do that.
The harder test, the one that distinguishes a serious power from a merely large one, is whether we can tell the difference between pressure and punishment, between coercion and cruelty, between strategic purpose and the exercise of force simply because the force is available.
Restraint is not weakness when restraint comes from understanding what power is _**for**_.
A superpower should judge coercion by what it changes, not by how much pain it can inflict. "We successfully made their civilians desperate" was never a victory condition. It is an indictment.
Eventually, when a policy keeps failing on its own terms, civilian suffering stops being the unfortunate cost of the strategy and becomes the strategy's most reliable accomplishment.
Iraq should have taught us to separate genuine constraint from strategic success. Cuba has had more than sixty years to teach us what happens when an instrument becomes an identity. Iran is now showing us how an authoritarian state can absorb economic warfare by routing a remarkable share of the damage into the lives of ordinary people.
We should not need another generation to learn the lesson.
Power sometimes requires coercion. Precisely because coercion can be necessary, a powerful country has an obligation to know what its coercion is for, who it actually reaches, whether it is working, and when to stop.
Moral restraint is not the alternative to serious strategy.
It is one of the disciplines that makes strategy serious.

What sanctions regimes on Iran, Iraq, and Cuba should have taught America about power. | | | Sep 18 | | | | | | | | | | | | Washington has a vocabulary problem. Let's start there. Every few years, a new administration announces another "economic onslaught." Another "financial stranglehold." Another "maximum pressure campaign." This time it is Iran, and the language coming out of Treasury recently has been almost cinematic: an "economic D-Day," a promise to sever "every economic lifeline" sustaining the regime. It is the same tone Mike Pompeo used in 2018, promising Iran "the strongest sanctions in history." It is the same register Barack Obama used in 2012, promising "even more crippling sanctions." Different administrations, different parties, the same metaphor: suffocation. But suffocation is a method. It is not an objective. And a superpower that stops asking the difference is not being tough; it is being lazy. Economic sanctions can do several different jobs. They can constrain access to weapons, technology, capital, or strategic inputs. They can deter third parties from assisting prohibited activity. They can freeze assets, disrupt patronage networks, signal international condemnation, or raise the cost of aggression. Sometimes those measures work even when the target government never changes its mind. But maximum-pressure campaigns make a larger claim. Their theory is not merely that economic restrictions will deny a particular component or interrupt a particular transaction. Their theory is that sufficiently severe economic pressure will change the political decisions of the targeted state. That is the claim we should evaluate on its merits. The question was never can America hurt Iran 's economy? Obviously yes. Iran's GDP is projected to contract by more than five percent this year. Inflation climbed from the low 50s to nearly 90% in a matter of months. The rial has collapsed in exchange rate value below two million to the dollar. That is real economic pain, and it is landing as serious poverty on millions of real families. The question that we're looking at today, is different, and it's the one the planners in in DC should have been evaluating this whole time: what political outcome do we intend for that suffering to produce, and why do we believe hurting these particular people will produce it? Increasingly, the answer appears to be that the transmission mechanism DC has been counting on is badly broken. Meaning, the US is inflicting mass suffering, on purpose, with no discernible strategic value, and no anticipated endpoint, at immense cost both to the Iranian people and to our moral and strategic position in the world. And we should know better. We've run versions of this experiment before, at enormous cost, without absorbing what they should have taught us. Let's get into it. Morality and strategy belong in the same room There is a habit in American foreign policy of treating the humanitarian objection as the "soft" one, the thing people raise when they have not quite grasped how power works. I want to reject that framing directly, because it gets the relationship between morality and strategy almost exactly backwards. Morality without strategy is useless sentiment. It can feel righteous and change nothing. Strategy without morality curdles into something worse than useless: callous cruelty wearing the costume of realism. Good statecraft requires both halves -- a legitimate objective and a method capable of reaching it at a cost proportionate to what can actually be gained. Ask a strategist what they need to know before backing a coercive policy, and the list should sound reasonably familiar. What is the objective? What mechanism connects this action to that objective? Who actually absorbs the cost? How will the adversary adapt? What happens to our alliances, credibility, and freedom of action along the way? At what point does the human toll exceed any plausible strategic return? Now ask the moral questions. Is the harm necessary? Is it falling primarily on people responsible for the conduct we are trying to change? Is the cost proportionate to the objective? Is there a less destructive means available? Is there a reasonable prospect of success? Those are not competing frameworks. Necessity, discrimination, proportionality, and a reasonable prospect of success sound like moral criteria because they are. They also sound remarkably like competent planning. Moral discipline is, among other things, a technology for preventing strategic stupidity. If your plan requires millions of civilians to suffer in the hope that their suffering will eventually change someone else's decision, asking whether that mechanism actually works is not sentimentality. It is the first question any serious strategist should ask. Iran: a state that learned to survive the blow Here is what the data on Iran's economy shows once you look past the headline numbers. Iran has spent more than a decade adapting to severe economic pressure. Before the current war, it kept oil flowing to China through sanctions-evasion networks. Currency depreciation made Iranian goods cheaper across the region, turning one economic weakness into an export advantage. Iranian firms, especially in sensitive industries such as electrical machinery, built inventories that can run close to 200 days deep. A blockade therefore does not necessarily stop production immediately; it begins by drawing down reserves accumulated for exactly this kind of disruption. Iranian policymakers also followed a very different path from Moscow. When Russia was hit with major sanctions after invading Ukraine, it responded with fiscal stimulus, industrial expansion, tighter labor markets, and rising wages -- something approaching a wartime mobilization of the domestic economy. Iran, on the other hand, tolerated inflation, ran austerity budgets, allowed weak labor conditions to suppress wages, and did relatively little to protect household purchasing power. It also declined to impose the kind of price controls that had helped shield civilians during the Iran-Iraq War. Whether every part of this outcome was deliberately engineered matters less than the fact that Iranian leaders have repeatedly demonstrated their willingness to tolerate it. The economic burden that DC is intending to impose on the capacity of decisionmakers in Tehran to maintain Iran's sovereignty, has instead migrated downward onto ordinary people. Households buy less. Firms pass costs onto consumers. People rely increasingly on credit and informal loans. Even food retailers report falling sales volume -- never a good sign. Meanwhile, the state has preserved greater access to the resources it considers essential. | | ---|---|--- The result is a genuinely ugly, but resilient, equilibrium. As households consume less, Iran needs fewer imports. As import demand falls, the state needs less foreign currency to keep the remaining economy functioning. Imports are on pace to fall from roughly $72 billion two years ago to around $40 billion this year. That is evidence of impoverishment. It is also, mechanically, one of the things allowing the system to remain functional while its people absorb the loss. None of that means sanctions have no effect. They damage growth, industrial development, household welfare, and Iran's long-term economic capacity. They can constrain access to particular goods and technologies. But none of those effects establishes that broad economic suffering will compel Tehran to make the political concessions Washington seeks. A country can become much poorer without becoming much more compliant. Pain is not leverage unless someone can transmit it This is the causal mechanism that too often disappears inside the phrase "economic pressure." Sanctions do not coerce governments by magic. Pressure has to travel through a political system. The implicit chain looks something like this: economic restrictions create losses; those losses fall on politically relevant actors; those actors pressure the leadership; the leadership concludes that continuing the challenged policy costs more than changing it; behavior changes. Break any link in that chain, and more pain does not necessarily produce more leverage. Authoritarian systems are unusually capable of breaking those links. They can shift scarcity toward households, protect favored constituencies, ration access to hard currency, suppress protest, censor information, scapegoat outsiders, and use coercive institutions to prevent public discontent from becoming elite constraint. They may be economically damaged while remaining politically insulated. That produces a fundamental problem for coercive strategy. The governments most willing to let their own citizens suffer are often the governments least susceptible to a strategy that depends on civilian suffering becoming politically intolerable. Sanctions generate pressure. Political transmission converts pressure into leverage. If the political system can prevent that pressure from reaching the people who make the decisions, increasing the pressure may increase suffering without increasing leverage. Iran is not the first place the US should have learned this. Iraq: the warning was more complicated -- and worse Iraq is not a simple story in which sanctions accomplished nothing. Saying so would make the argument easier to write and easier to knock down. After Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait in 1990, the UN Security Council imposed one of the most comprehensive sanctions regimes of the modern era. Those measures did constrain Saddam Hussein's capabilities. Combined with inspections, international monitoring, and the threat of military force, they contributed to the dismantlement and degradation of weapons programs that Washington would later badly misunderstand. From a cold strategic perspective, the sanctions were partially effective. But look at the cost. Sanctions on Iraq remained in place, in varying forms, for thirteen years. Iraqi economic and civic life deteriorated so severely that the international community created the Oil-for-Food program to mitigate the humanitarian consequences while attempting to preserve strategic pressure. Saddam's government contributed substantially to the catastrophe through repression, corruption, misallocation, and its manipulation of relief. The destruction of the Gulf War and Iraq's degraded infrastructure compounded the damage. But the central political fact remained: Saddam Hussein stayed in power. That should have forced a harder conversation about what exactly the sanctions regime was accomplishing and at what price. It constrained Iraqi state capacity, but it did not reliably convert civilian deprivation into political moderation. Sometimes it survives for decades. The third is a failure of legitimacy. Everyone else is watching, and they draw conclusions about how the United States uses power, whether DC can be trusted, and whether they might be next. That third failure feeds the second. America's ability to organize coalitions depends largely on other governments believing that we exercise power with restraint, that our stated rules are more than convenient rhetoric, that civilian welfare actually enters into our decisions, and that cooperation with us does not mean surrendering indefinitely to whatever policy Washington may choose next. Moral credibility is not decorative trim on American power. It is a core, structural part of American power. Countries cooperate with us not only because we are strong, but because alliances, institutions, law, reputation, trust, and perceived legitimacy reduce the cost of getting other actors to move with us. Legitimacy is force multiplication. Hypocrisy creates strategic friction. If the visible result of American policy is that ordinary people become markedly poorer while the target government retains enough power to continue the conduct we intended to stop, other countries do not need to adopt Tehran's worldview to question Washington's judgment. The bill comes due somewhere else The same problem reaches beyond the targeted country. When Washington leans heavily on dollar dominance, correspondent banking, market access, and secondary sanctions as instruments of coercion, other governments are not only asking whether Iran deserves the pressure. They are also asking what their own dependence on American-controlled financial infrastructure could mean under a future disagreement. That anxiety now appears regularly in BRICS diplomacy and throughout parts of the Global South. At the most recent summit, BRICS leaders again condemned unilateral sanctions imposed outside the framework of the UN Security Council. The declaration did not name Washington, but American and Western sanctions architecture has long been one of the grievances animating that conversation. BRICS countries are not a unified anti-American bloc. India, Brazil, South Africa, China, Russia, and the bloc's newer members have different interests and often different views of the international order. Nor is the dollar about to vanish, although several meaningful global trade structures are being built to reduce global dependency on financial infrastructure DC controls. Bottom line: every American use of financial dominance as a weapon teaches other governments something about the risk of depending on the system through which that weapon operates. The rational response is diversification: more local-currency settlement, more alternative payment infrastructure, more trading relationships insulated from Western jurisdiction, more reserve diversification, and more political interest in institutions Washington cannot easily control. Whether or not this leads to a sudden collapse of dollar dominance, it is clearly a long-term strategic cost. We are spending down our strongest global form of enduring power carelessly, even recklessly, and assuming we can go on doing so forever. That's foolish. America is spending financial leverage faster than we are rebuilding the legitimacy that helps sustain it. The dictator's bargain Across Iraq, Cuba, and now Iran, the same political mechanism keeps appearing. Washington tells the population: your suffering is your government 's fault. The government tells its population: your suffering is Washington 's fault. Frustratingly, both sides can often produce evidence. The authoritarian government made bad choices, repressed its population, distorted its economy, or pursued policies that invited external pressure. The outside power then imposed policies that made ordinary life materially worse. One source of suffering does not erase the other. That ambiguity is a gift to authoritarian rulers. It gives them an external villain who is at least partly real. It also exposes a contradiction in the coercive theory. We tell an oppressed population that its government does not care whether it suffers, and then make civilian economic suffering a central mechanism by which we expect that government to change its behavior. The less accountable the government is to its population, the weaker that transmission mechanism becomes. This does not mean authoritarian leaders are immune to economic pressure. They care about elite cohesion, patronage networks, military capability, state revenue, access to strategic technology, and their own survival. Those are real pressure points. But that is exactly why serious strategy should identify and attack the relevant pressure point specifically, rather than treating generalized national misery as a proxy for leverage. What better strategy actually looks like None of this is an argument for unilateral disarmament, and it should not be mistaken for one. States sometimes need coercive tools. Sanctions can constrain dangerous capabilities, freeze assets, raise costs, disrupt procurement, punish specific actors, and support broader diplomatic or security objectives. The requirement is more demanding than "targeted sanctions good, broad sanctions bad." Targeted measures are often more defensible because they discriminate better between decision-makers and civilians, but they are not automatically effective at compelling political change. The real principle is simpler: match the instrument to the mechanism. If the objective is to prevent acquisition of a weapons component, target the component, supplier, financing channel, and logistics network. If the objective is to disrupt elite patronage, target the assets and institutions on which that patronage depends. If the objective is to change behavior, identify the person or coalition capable of changing it and build pressure around what that actor values. Then build an off-ramp. A coercive policy without a credible path to relief easily becomes punishment without strategy. The target must know what behavior is being demanded, what compliance would look like, what partial compliance earns, and what actions actually cause sanctions to end. Otherwise the pressure tends to become permanent -- because permanence is bureaucratically easier than declaring success, admitting failure, or renegotiating the objective. Humanitarian protections also have to work outside the text of a Treasury regulation. Formal exemptions for food and medicine are not enough if banks, insurers, freight companies, pharmaceutical suppliers, and intermediaries conclude that touching the sanctioned economy creates unacceptable compliance risk. A humanitarian exemption that no functioning financial institution is willing to process is an exemption on paper, not a real humanitarian channel that helps people. Protected payment mechanisms, credible safe harbors, clear licensing, and active monitoring of real-world access have to be part of the design. And every major sanctions regime should face periodic review -- scheduled, not optional -- built around questions so obvious that it is remarkable how rarely they organize the public debate: Who exactly must change what behavior? Why should this specific pressure make that actor change it? Who is actually absorbing the cost? What capabilities are being constrained? What evidence would show that the policy is succeeding? What evidence would show that it is failing? What is the humanitarian ceiling? What is the exit condition? If the architects cannot answer those questions, that is an answer. A superpower capable of restraint A superpower does not prove its strength by demonstrating that it can impoverish people who cannot meaningfully fight back. We already know we can do that. Everyone knows we can do that. The harder test, the one that distinguishes a serious power from a merely large one, is whether we can tell the difference between pressure and punishment, between coercion and cruelty, between strategic purpose and the exercise of force simply because the force is available. Restraint is not weakness when restraint comes from understanding what power is for**. A superpower should judge coercion by what it changes, not by how much pain it can inflict. "We successfully made their civilians desperate" was never a victory condition. It is an indictment. Eventually, when a policy keeps failing on its own terms, civilian suffering stops being the unfortunate cost of the strategy and becomes the strategy's most reliable accomplishment. Iraq should have taught us to separate genuine constraint from strategic success. Cuba has had more than sixty years to teach us what happens when an instrument becomes an identity. Iran is now showing us how an authoritarian state can absorb economic warfare by routing a remarkable share of the damage into the lives of ordinary people. We should not need another generation to learn the lesson. Power sometimes requires coercion. Precisely because coercion can be necessary, a powerful country has an obligation to know what its coercion is for, who it actually reaches, whether it is working, and when to stop. Moral restraint is not the alternative to serious strategy. It is one of the disciplines that makes strategy serious. Let me be honest with you about something.
I'm not supposed to be in this race.
The grandson of a sharecropper? Not supposed to be a viable Senate candidate in Louisiana.
A Black farmer from rural Tensas Parish? Not supposed to compete statewide in the Deep South.
Someone without billionaire backers or a Rolodex full of Washington insiders? Not supposed to have a shot at flipping a Senate seat.
But here we are.
**And MAGA is absolutely shocked.**
They thought Louisiana was locked up. They thought they could focus on defending seats in swing states while the South stayed safely red. They thought a race like ours — a real populist challenge to their grip on power — wasn't possible here.
They were wrong.
Look at what's happening: Democrats flipping Trump districts across the South. MAGA candidates tearing each other apart in primaries. Republican retirements at levels not seen since the Great Depression. Trump's approval cratering over his failed Iran war.
This is a once-in-a-lifetime opening. The kind of moment that doesn't come around often in Louisiana politics.
**_And I believe — deep in my bones — that this is the campaign to meet this moment._**
Not because I'm the most polished politician. Not because I've been planning a Senate run my whole career. But because I understand what working Louisianans need because I've lived their struggles.
I know what it's like to watch costs rise while your income stays flat. I know what it's like to compete against corporations that rig the system against family operations. I know what it's like to worry about whether there will be anything left for the next generation.
That's the authentic economic populism that can win here. Not the fake MAGA version that delivers nothing but culture wars — the real thing that actually fights for working people.
And if we capitalize on this moment — if we show the political world that Louisiana is genuinely winnable — everything changes.
Not just for this race. For the entire map. For what's possible in the South.
But only if we have the resources to compete. And that counts on good folks like you stepping up.

clean_body: MAGA is shocked we're competitive. A Black farmer from rural Louisiana isn't supposed to threaten their Senate seat. But here we are. | | | = Let me be honest with you about something. I'm not supposed to be in this race. The grandson of a sharecropper? Not supposed to be a viable Senate candidate in Louisiana. A Black farmer from rural Tensas Parish? Not supposed to compete statewide in the Deep South. Someone without billionaire backers or a Rolodex full of Washington insiders? Not supposed to have a shot at flipping a Senate seat. But here we are. And MAGA is absolutely shocked. They thought Louisiana was locked up. They thought they could focus on defending seats in swing states while the South stayed safely red. They thought a race like ours — a real populist challenge to their grip on power — wasn't possible here. They were wrong. Look at what's happening: Democrats flipping Trump districts across the South. MAGA candidates tearing each other apart in primaries. Republican retirements at levels not seen since the Great Depression. Trump's approval cratering over his failed Iran war. This is a once-in-a-lifetime opening. The kind of moment that doesn't come around often in Louisiana politics. And I believe — deep in my bones — that this is the campaign to meet this moment. Not because I'm the most polished politician. Not because I've been planning a Senate run my whole career. But because I understand what working Louisianans need because I've lived their struggles. I know what it's like to watch costs rise while your income stays flat. I know what it's like to compete against corporations that rig the system against family operations. I know what it's like to worry about whether there will be anything left for the next generation. That's the authentic economic populism that can win here. And if we capitalize on this moment — if we show the political world that Louisiana is genuinely winnable — everything changes. Not just for this race. For the entire map.
